research_text:
## API and reported value

`java.security.SecureRandom` provides cryptographically strong random-number generation. Oracle says seed material supplied to it must be unpredictable. The reported constructor finding concerns the **seed byte array** passed to `SecureRandom(byte[])`, not the array later filled by `nextBytes(byte[])`. The CrySL rule requires the seed to satisfy its `randomized` predicate; the rule does not itself define how a detector establishes that fact. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/SecureRandom.html?utm_source=openai))

Oracle API: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/SecureRandom.html

## Documented safe usage and remediation

Oracle documents obtaining an instance with the no-argument constructor or a `getInstance` method, then calling `nextBytes` to fill an array. For a newly created **PRNG** instance, the first `nextBytes` call causes self-seeding from an implementation-specific entropy source, unless `setSeed` was called previously. If a caller supplies seed material, Oracle requires it to be unpredictable and, for early `setSeed`, to contain enough entropy for the generator’s security. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/SecureRandom.html?utm_source=openai))

Accordingly, the documented alternatives to supplying unsuitable seed material are to use the self-seeding pattern or supply unpredictable, sufficiently entropic seed material. Oracle also documents `generateSeed(int)` for obtaining seed bytes for other generators. This is API usage guidance; the sources do not prescribe a finding-specific remediation procedure. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/SecureRandom.html?utm_source=openai))

For both `setSeed` overloads, Oracle says the supplied seed supplements rather than replaces existing seed and repeated calls never reduce randomness. The CrySL predicate is nevertheless required for every modeled `setSeed` input, regardless of that timing distinction. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/SecureRandom.html?utm_source=openai))

## Compatibility and migration

- **Platform versions:** `SecureRandom` has existed since Java 1.1; `getInstanceStrong()` is documented since Java 8, and `reseed()` since Java 9. Not every implementation supports `reseed()`. Algorithm and provider availability also vary. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/SecureRandom.html))
- **Output compatibility:** Oracle describes many implementations as deterministic generators initialized from a seed, while the default constructor selects an implementation through providers. The API does **not** promise that changing seeding or providers preserves an earlier output sequence. Whether any stored value depends on reproducing such a sequence is unresolved. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/SecureRandom.html?utm_source=openai))
- **Persisted and wire formats:** Oracle documents `SecureRandom` as serializable and publishes its serialized form, but the reviewed sources do not specify how a seeding change affects an application’s persisted data or wire format. Nor do they provide a general migration path for data dependent on an earlier sequence. Those compatibility questions require information outside the supplied scope. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/serialized-form.html))

Serialized-form reference: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/serialized-form.html

## Exact CrySL rule

The cited file declares `SPEC java.security.SecureRandom`. Its constructor event and seed requirement are written as follows; the intervening declarations are omitted here, not altered: ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SecureRandom.crysl))

```text
byte[] seed;
```

```text
c2: SecureRandom(seed);
```

```text
REQUIRES
	randomized[seed];
```

The file also declares `setSeed(seed)` and `setSeed(lSeed)`, with `lSeed` declared as `long` and subject to `randomized[lSeed]`. Thus, for the reported constructor event, the rule specifies **one byte-array parameter** and requires `randomized` for that bound value. This is a rule predicate, not a runtime entropy test described by the file. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SecureRandom.crysl))

The other named events are `SecureRandom()`, `getInstance` with one or two arguments, `getInstanceStrong()`, `generateSeed`, `nextBytes`, and zero- and one-argument `nextInt`. The two-argument `getInstance` event has an unconstrained second argument; the algorithm value is separately restricted to the six names in the file. The events are declared under the `java.security.SecureRandom` specification—not as a general name-only matching clause. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SecureRandom.crysl))

**A method merely sharing one of those names is not stated by this source to match.** The file does not specify the detector’s receiver/subtype resolution semantics, so its actual treatment of a particular unrelated or subtype call cannot be established from this file alone. The supplied URL tracks `master`; the reviewed page alone does not establish that its bytes match the reported SHA-256. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SecureRandom.crysl))
